t.7.8.2: Then the night-roamer, his eyes reddened with rage and his crown shaking from anger, spoke these harsh words to Padmanābha.
t.7.8.1: Then, as that army was being struck down from behind by Padmanābha, Mālyavān turned back, like the ocean turning back after it has surged beyond its shore.
t.7.8.3: O Nārāyaṇa, you do not know the eternal code of the warrior, you who strike us down like a common man, though we are broken and have no mind to fight.
t.7.8.4: O lord of the gods, whoever commits the sin of slaying one whose face is turned away, that slayer, when he has departed, does not attain the heaven of those whose deeds are virtuous.
t.7.8.5: Or if you have a desire for battle, O bearer of the conch, discus and mace, here I stand; I am watching, so show whatever strength is yours.
t.7.8.6: The mighty younger brother of the king of the gods said to that lord of the rākṣasas: “To the gods, terrified out of fear of you, I have indeed granted safety, the extermination of the rākṣasas, and that very promise is now being kept.”
t.7.8.7: What is dear to the gods must always be done by me, even at the cost of my life; so I shall slay you, even if you have fled to Rasātala.
t.7.8.8: But as the god with eyes like red lotuses was speaking thus, the enraged lord of the rākṣasas pierced him with his spear and roared aloud.
t.7.8.9: The spear hurled from the arm of Mālyavān, its bells ringing out, blazed upon the chest of Hari like lightning resting in a cloud.
t.7.8.10: Then the lotus-eyed one, dear to the bearer of the spear, pulled out that very spear and hurled it, aiming at Mālyavān.
t.7.8.11: That spear, hurled from the hand of Govinda as if released by Skanda, sped toward the rākṣasa, eager for him, like a great meteor falling upon the Añjana mountain.
t.7.8.12: It fell upon the broad chest of that lord of the Rākṣasas, which gleamed with the radiance of his necklace, like a thunderbolt falling upon a mountain peak.
t.7.8.14: Then, seizing a spear of black iron studded with many thorns, he struck the god forcefully between the breasts.
t.7.8.13: His armour pierced through by it, he sank into a deep darkness; then Mālyavān, recovering once more, stood firm like an immovable mountain.
t.7.8.15: In just the same way, the night-roamer, impassioned for battle, struck the younger brother of Vāsava with his fist and withdrew a bow's length away.
t.7.8.16: Then a great cry of "Well done, well done!" arose in the sky, as the Rākṣasa, having struck Viṣṇu, smote Garuḍa as well.
t.7.8.17: Then Vainateya, enraged, drove the rākṣasa away with the wind of his wings, as a mighty wind sweeps away a heap of dry leaves.
t.7.8.18: Seeing his elder brother driven off by the wind of the lord of birds' wings, Sumālī set out toward Laṅkā together with his own forces.
t.7.8.19: The rākṣasa Mālyavān too, blown away by the force of the wind from Garuḍa's wings, rejoined his own forces and went to Laṅkā, overcome with shame.
t.7.8.20: Thus, O lotus-eyed Rāma, those Rākṣasas, their foremost leaders slain, were many times shattered in battle by Hari.
t.7.8.21: Unable to fight back against Viṣṇu and stricken with fear, they abandoned Laṅkā and went with their wives to dwell in Pātāla.
t.7.8.22: O delight of the Raghus, having rallied around the Rākṣasa Sumālin, those warriors of renowned valor remained in the lineage of Sālakaṭaṃkaṭa.
t.7.8.24: O conqueror of cities, there is no other slayer of the Rākṣasas, even among the gods, except the god Nārāyaṇa, who bears the conch, the discus and the mace.
t.7.8.23: Those rākṣasas who were slain by you were indeed known as Paulastyas; but Sumālī, Mālyavant, Mālī, and those who went before them as their leaders, all these, O illustrious one, were mightier than Rāvaṇa.
t.7.8.25: You are the god Nārāyaṇa, four-armed and eternal, born to slay the Rākṣasas, the unconquerable and imperishable Lord.
